notes.b: Unpaid work is the work done in and around the home without any wage. It keeps households running and spares families the cost of paying for services.
points: Unpaid work covers child care, housework, cooking, laundry, caring for an elderly parent or a person with a disability, gardening, household management, and DIY and home maintenance.
It is done mainly within the household, without financial reward and often out of family duty, so it is not a free choice in the way voluntary work is.
It keeps households and the community functioning and supports the paid workforce, because children and workers are cared for and fed. In this way it makes family life possible.
Because it is unpaid, it saves families the cost of paying for these services themselves, such as child care or home help.
It is not counted in measures of national paid output and has no wage, pension entitlement or sick pay of its own, so its contribution is often overlooked.
Unpaid work can be monotonous, and it often falls unequally on women within the household.
Carers can become isolated or stressed, because looking after a relative can take up most of the day.
notes.tip: Unpaid home work is a type of work, but it is not voluntary work. Keep the two apart in your answer: unpaid work is done within the home, with no pay, and may not be by choice.

notes.b: Many people look after a relative at home. They are unpaid carers, and the care they give matters to both families and the State.
points: Unpaid carers look after relatives at home, such as an older person or a person with a disability. They are often helped by State supports such as carer's payments.
They save the State and families large costs, because the care would otherwise have to be paid for through nursing homes, home help or hospital services.
They give care in a familiar home setting, which is often more comfortable for the person being cared for.
notes.tip: Exams ask about the roles of unpaid carers in the community. Give the cost saving to the State and families and the care in a familiar setting.

notes.b: Voluntary work is unpaid work done freely, by choice, for people or a cause outside the household, usually through an organisation.
points: The volunteer gets no wage, sick pay or pension, but expenses for travel or training may be repaid.

Voluntary work is carried out through charities, community groups, sports clubs, schools, parish and church groups, youth organisations and local development groups. St Vincent de Paul is one example: a national voluntary agency using church-gate collections, charity shops and local visiting.

Typical activities include running charity shops, fundraising, providing meals on wheels and transport for older people, visiting the housebound, and mentoring and coaching young people as club coaches or youth leaders.
Other activities include running local events, community clean-ups, first aid and emergency or rescue services, and community care and support groups.
Environmental volunteering includes litter clean-ups, tree planting, conservation work and local recycling projects.
Volunteers need training, and Garda vetting through the organisation for work with children or vulnerable adults, so that those they help are protected.
notes.tip: Work experience placements and internships are unpaid but are not voluntary work as the syllabus means it. Do not call volunteering free labour or a substitute for paid work, because it complements paid services.

notes.h: Difference between unpaid home work and voluntary work
notes.b: Both kinds of work are unpaid and neither is employment, but they differ in why, for whom and how they are done.
points: Unpaid home work is largely a duty within the family, whereas voluntary work is chosen freely.
Unpaid home work benefits the household, whereas voluntary work benefits people and causes in the wider community.
Voluntary work is usually organised through an organisation, whereas home work is usually carried out individually.
notes.tip: Questions ask you to explain or differentiate unpaid and voluntary work. Use chosen versus duty, and community versus household, and say that voluntary work is often with a charity.

notes.b: Volunteers give their time without pay, but they gain a great deal themselves. These benefits are personal, practical and social.
points: Skills and experience such as teamwork, communication, organisation and leadership, plus training, can be listed on a CV and used for a reference.
Confidence and self-esteem grow as the volunteer contributes to something valued, giving a sense of purpose and achievement.
Social contact and friendships bring a feeling of belonging and reduce isolation, particularly for people who are retired, unemployed or new to an area.
Volunteering gives people a sense of purpose and fulfilment, and a chance to develop their potential.
Volunteering can lead to paid employment, or to expertise in a particular area, as it builds experience and references in that field.
Empathy and insight into the lives of others develop through helping people in need, such as older or vulnerable people.
Volunteering keeps people active and healthy, and is a good use of free time for people who are retired or between jobs.
notes.tip: Benefits to the volunteer and benefits to the community are different lists. Keep them separate, and develop three or four points with a reason each. For fulfilling their potential, give reward and fulfilment, new skills, insight into others' lives and confidence.

notes.b: The community gains services, support and a stronger sense of belonging from the people who give their time. These benefits are separate from what the volunteers themselves gain.
points: Services that would otherwise be unavailable or unaffordable can be provided, such as meals for older or housebound people, transport, youth clubs, sports coaching and support groups.
Support for vulnerable groups, including older people, people with disabilities, lone parents, the homeless, people at risk of poverty and new arrivals, reaches those who might otherwise be missed.
Volunteers build community spirit and social cohesion by bringing people from different backgrounds together around a shared purpose.
Where young people are involved in clubs there is less crime and vandalism, because they have something positive to do.
Local facilities such as halls, pitches and parks are built, maintained and improved through volunteer effort and fundraising.
Volunteering saves the State and local bodies money and complements paid services, though it does not replace them.
Volunteers raise awareness of local issues and encourage participation (civic participation) and active citizenship in decisions that affect the area.
notes.tip: Do not answer a question on benefits to the community with benefits to the volunteer. Develop three or four points from this list, each with its reason.

notes.h: Voluntary work and social and environmental change
notes.b: Volunteers do more than provide services. Their work changes how a community lives and how it treats its surroundings.
points: Social change: volunteers campaign for services and for the rights of groups, and help people to claim the supports they are entitled to.
Social change: volunteer-run projects build inclusion by supporting people with disabilities, minorities, Travellers and migrants to take part in community life, and they reduce isolation.
Environmental change: litter picks, clean-ups of rivers and beaches, tree planting and conservation work reduce litter and protect habitats such as woodland, river banks and coastline.
Environmental change: community gardens and growing schemes, recycling projects and local heritage projects change local habits and reduce waste.
The Tidy Towns competition is a well-known example of a community improvement effort driven by local volunteers.
Long-term change comes from volunteers passing on their knowledge and skills to others, so the work continues beyond any one project.
notes.tip: For how voluntary work contributes to social and environmental change, cover both: improved services and inclusion and community spirit, and litter and conservation projects.

notes.h: Limits and challenges of voluntary work
notes.b: Voluntary work depends on people's goodwill and spare time, which creates some limits.
points: Volunteers can experience burnout when a few people carry a large share of the work.
Groups depend on continued volunteer commitment, which can be hard to sustain as people take on paid work or family responsibilities.
Volunteers can face out-of-pocket costs for travel, equipment or training that are not reimbursed.
Volunteers are not employees, so they have no pay, sick pay or pension.
Volunteers need training, and Garda vetting for work with children or vulnerable adults.

notes.b: Volunteering is helped along by national organisations and by ways of encouraging people to take part.
points: Volunteer Ireland is the national volunteer development organisation, supporting Volunteer Centres and running National Volunteering Week. The first national strategy, the National Volunteering Strategy, was published by the Government in December 2020. Its period ended in 2025, so a successor may exist.
Volunteering can be encouraged through training, recognition and repaying expenses, which helps to remove the out-of-pocket costs that put people off.
notes.tip: Exams ask about the roles of voluntary organisations in the community and ways to encourage volunteering. Training, recognition and expenses are the points to give.

keyTerms.definition: Work done without financial reward, mainly in the home, such as child care, housework and caring for relatives.
Unpaid work done by choice for the benefit of people or causes outside the household.
A person who gives unpaid time to voluntary work through a charity, community group or organisation.
The sense of belonging and mutual trust that draws people in a community together.
Taking part in community life and public decisions, such as through local groups and consultations.
Physical and emotional exhaustion caused by sustained pressure, often when a few people carry most of a group's work.
The ability to understand and share the feelings of others, developed through helping people in need.
Bringing people at risk of isolation or disadvantage into full participation in community life.

factCards.definition: No financial reward; done mainly in the home; includes child care, housework and care of elderly or disabled relatives.
New skills and experience; confidence and self-esteem; social contact and friendships; a sense of purpose and fulfilment.
Services that would otherwise be unavailable; social cohesion between different groups; support for vulnerable people such as older people and lone parents.
Litter clean-ups, tree planting, habitat conservation on riverbanks and coastline, and local recycling schemes.

factCards.term: How voluntary work differs from home work
factCards.definition: Voluntary work is chosen freely, is done for people outside the household, and is usually organised through a group or organisation.
Burnout when a few people carry most of the work; difficulty sustaining commitment as volunteers take on paid work or family responsibilities.

questions.prompt: Describe two ways in which voluntary work benefits a local community.
questions.model: Voluntary work provides services that would otherwise be unavailable or unaffordable, such as meals or transport for older people. It also builds social cohesion, bringing people from different backgrounds together around a shared purpose.

questions.prompt: Discuss how voluntary work can benefit the volunteer personally, and evaluate its contribution to social and environmental change in a local community.
questions.model: Personal benefits include new skills such as teamwork and leadership, growth in confidence and self-esteem, friendships that reduce isolation, and a sense of purpose. Volunteering can also develop empathy and build experience that supports paid employment. For the community, volunteers campaign for better local services and promote social inclusion of people with disabilities or from minority groups. Environmental contributions include clean-ups, habitat conservation and recycling schemes that change local habits. The contribution is limited by burnout when a few people carry most of the work and by difficulty sustaining volunteer commitment over time.
